note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: When the target is absent and the floor value repeats, which index is wanted?
What should be returned if every element is larger than target?
Can the array be empty?
hints: Both answers are determined by the first index whose value is >= target.
Maintain a half-open range [lo, hi) and move lo past values smaller than target.
At the end lo is the lower bound: return lo if arr[lo]==target, otherwise lo-1.
invariants: every index < lo holds a value < target
every index >= hi holds a value >= target
chooseWhen: The array is sorted and many lookups or large inputs make O(n) scans too slow
tradeoffs: Binary search needs random access; a linear scan is simpler for tiny arrays
hack2hire:67955715010c9ed2f849b1f7.variantLabel: Inferred: first occurrence, else floor index

clarifyingQuestions: Is any valid tree accepted, or a specific shape?
How are equal counts ordered?
What is returned for an empty string?
hints: The leaf counts are just character frequencies.
Every merge creates a parent whose count is the sum of two nodes; merging the two smallest gives a Huffman tree.
Key a min-heap by (count, creation id) so ties break the same way in every language.
invariants: each pool entry is the root of a valid subtree
creation ids are unique and increasing
chooseWhen: A deterministic frequency tree is needed, for example as a prefix-code tree
tradeoffs: A heap costs O(log d) per merge; with d <= 52 even repeated sorting is cheap
hack2hire:68f012a4742c37be9dc830dd.variantLabel: Inferred: Huffman-style merge tree with deterministic ties

constraints: timestamps are decimal strings without leading zeros, below 2**53
clarifyingQuestions: Should the result be a nested map or a list of edges?
Are timestamps compared numerically or as strings?
Does a user with one entry produce START->r and r->END?
hints: Each user contributes an independent path.
Sort each user path by numeric timestamp, not by string.
Add virtual START and END around every path and count adjacent pairs in a map keyed by (from, to).
invariants: every user contributes exactly len(path)+1 transitions
edge counts only increase
chooseWhen: Logs are unordered and grouped per user
tradeoffs: Sorting per user costs O(n log n); bucketed timestamps would need a bounded range
hack2hire:6a222b9c981072682a6f1e5a.variantLabel: Inferred: transition counts as sorted triples

clarifyingQuestions: Are orders processed in input order?
Is a partly satisfiable order skipped entirely?
Should the answer be a count or per-order flags?
hints: Each order only depends on the stock left by earlier orders.
Check all three types before deducting anything.
Keep three counters; deduct only when all three checks pass.
invariants: remaining stock is never negative
chooseWhen: Orders must be served in arrival order
tradeoffs: Greedy arrival order does not maximise the number of fulfilled orders

constraints: up to 20000 assignments, each with at most 8 terms
literals 0..999999, variable names 1-10 characters starting with a letter
every value stays within 1e15 in magnitude
clarifyingQuestions: Which operators may appear in an expression?
Can an assignment reference a variable defined later in the array?
What if a variable is undefined or defined in terms of itself?
hints: Treat the assignments as a dependency graph.
Evaluate a variable only after all variables it references.
Use an explicit stack for the DFS: chains can be 20000 deep.
invariants: a memoised value never changes
a variable is evaluated once
chooseWhen: Only one target value is needed from many assignments
tradeoffs: DFS evaluates only what the target needs; topological order evaluates everything
hack2hire:68811ae3f96758aa78e1d687.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: sums of literals and variables

constraints: up to 20000 assignments, each with at most 8 terms
literals 0..999999, variable names 1-10 characters starting with a letter
every value stays within 1e15 in magnitude
clarifyingQuestions: Which operators may appear in an expression?
Can an assignment reference a variable defined later in the array?
What if a variable is undefined or defined in terms of itself?
hints: Store each operand with its sign.
Left-to-right + and - equals summing signed operands.
Reuse the iterative memoised DFS from level 1.
invariants: a memoised value never changes
partial sums stay below 2**53
chooseWhen: Expressions mix addition and subtraction only
tradeoffs: No precedence handling is needed; multiplication would require a real parser

constraints: up to 20000 assignments, each with at most 8 terms
literals 0..999999, variable names 1-10 characters starting with a letter
every value stays within 1e15 in magnitude
clarifyingQuestions: Which operators may appear in an expression?
Can an assignment reference a variable defined later in the array?
What if a variable is undefined or defined in terms of itself?
Is a cycle that the target does not use an error?
hints: A failure anywhere below the target makes the target fail.
Colour nodes white/grey/black; meeting a grey node means a cycle.
Record failure as a memoised state so shared subgraphs are not re-explored.
invariants: grey nodes are exactly the current DFS path
black nodes have a final value or a final failure
chooseWhen: Inputs may be malformed and must be rejected without crashing
tradeoffs: Three-colour DFS detects cycles in one pass; fixed-point iteration is simpler but quadratic
hack2hire:68813e86f96758aa78e1d69b.variantLabel: Inferred level 3: detect undefined and cyclic references

clarifyingQuestions: Is waiting time measured from time 0 until completion minus own work?
Do all tasks arrive at time 0?
Is the answer a total or a per-task list?
hints: Simulation is too slow when hours are large: count instead.
Before task i starts its last hour, every task j has run min(a_j, a_i - 1) hours.
In the last round, task i also waits for earlier tasks with a_j >= a_i; count them with a Fenwick tree.
invariants: Fenwick prefix sums equal counts of already-seen tasks by value rank
chooseWhen: Many tasks with large hour counts
tradeoffs: O(n log n) with sorting; the literal simulation is O(sum of hours)

clarifyingQuestions: May a moving elevator take a call in the opposite direction?
Is an elevator at the passenger floor eligible?
How are ties broken?
hints: Decide eligibility independently for each elevator.
A moving elevator only helps if it has not passed the passenger yet in the call direction.
Track the smallest distance, updating only on strict improvement so the lowest index wins ties.
invariants: best holds the lowest-index eligible elevator with minimal distance so far
chooseWhen: One request against a snapshot of elevator states
tradeoffs: Per-request scan is O(n); many requests would call for indexing by floor

clarifyingQuestions: Are query timestamps non-decreasing too?
Can different users record at the same second?
What does a query for an unknown user or chat return?
hints: Only the last m seconds matter for any future query.
Because time never goes back, expired events can be dropped forever.
Keep a queue per user and pop its front while it is older than timestamp-m+1.
invariants: each user queue is sorted and contains only events that may still count
chooseWhen: Long-running counters with monotone time
tradeoffs: Queues store each event once; bucketed counters would bound memory by m

clarifyingQuestions: Are query timestamps non-decreasing too?
Can different users record at the same second?
What does a query for an unknown user or chat return?
Do chat counts include every user?
hints: A chat is just another key with its own queue.
Chat queues may hold equal timestamps from different users.
Evict with the same rule as user queues.
invariants: each queue is non-decreasing and holds only possibly-counting events
chooseWhen: Several independent rolling counts over one event stream
tradeoffs: Two queues double memory; a single event log would need per-key scans

clarifyingQuestions: Are query timestamps non-decreasing too?
Can different users record at the same second?
What does a query for an unknown user or chat return?
Is a user with several events in the window counted once?
hints: Distinct counting needs multiplicities, not just a set.
When an event leaves the window decrement its user; delete at zero.
The answer is the size of the multiplicity map after eviction.
invariants: map size equals the number of distinct users with events in the chat queue
chooseWhen: Distinct counts over sliding windows
tradeoffs: Exact multiplicity maps use O(window) memory; sketches would be approximate
hack2hire:6a579fe5665efda9311f9377.variantLabel: Inferred level 3: distinct active users per chat

clarifyingQuestions: Is the input a single pair or a batch?
Does z wrap to a?
Can each character be incremented at most once?
hints: Each character of new can stand for itself or its successor.
Matching the next old character as early as possible never hurts.
Walk new once with a pointer into old.
invariants: old[:j] is matched within the scanned prefix of new
chooseWhen: Subsequence checks with per-character alternatives
tradeoffs: Greedy is linear; the DP is quadratic but checks the greedy argument

clarifyingQuestions: Is 1 prime?
How are rotations with a leading zero read?
What is the bound on n?
hints: A number with any even digit or 5 (beyond one digit) cannot qualify; not required but a quick filter.
Rotate by moving the top digit: r = (r mod 10^(d-1)) * 10 + leading digit.
Trial division up to sqrt(r) is fast enough for r < 1e9.
invariants: each rotation is tested exactly once
chooseWhen: Single numbers below about 1e12
tradeoffs: Trial division is simple; Miller-Rabin is faster for large n

clarifyingQuestions: What does the second request type look like and return?
May a block wrap past the last slot?
Is the scan order startIndex, startIndex+1, ...?
hints: A block may wrap around the end.
Scan offsets from startIndex while counting consecutive free slots.
When the run reaches numberOfSlots, the block starts numberOfSlots-1 offsets back.
invariants: run = number of consecutive free slots ending at the current offset, counted from startIndex
chooseWhen: Small circular buffers with first-fit placement
tradeoffs: Linear scans are simple; interval trees would help for huge slot counts
hack2hire:6a1f2f7c8b879849ebc10f9a.variantLabel: Inferred: circular first-fit store and range free

clarifyingQuestions: How much energy does moving to the next house cost?
Does house 0 also cost energy?
Can Alex stop before the last house?
hints: Energy above the number of remaining moves is useless, so cap it.
State = energy after the choice at house i; value = best coins.
Transition both choices, then pay 1 energy to move; the answer is the best value at any house.
invariants: dp[e] is the best coin total with exactly e (capped) energy at the current house
chooseWhen: Small n with large energies
tradeoffs: O(n^2) DP; enumeration is exponential
hack2hire:6a4ffdfb665efda9311f57f2.variantLabel: Inferred: maximise coins with 1 energy per move

clarifyingQuestions: Is the step count or the sequence wanted?
Are there many queries (memoisation)?
What is the bound on n?
hints: Count transitions, not visited values.
Trajectory values can exceed n by far; check they stay exact.
For many queries, memoise steps of values below a limit.
invariants: steps counts applied transitions
chooseWhen: Single queries
tradeoffs: A memo table speeds repeated queries at memory cost
hack2hire:68d833b5ae12841706c1fc58.variantLabel: Inferred: Collatz step count for one n

clarifyingQuestions: Is the answer taken modulo a prime?
What if n = 1 and the colours differ?
Can k be 1?
hints: Only whether the current house has the last colour matters.
Two-state recurrence: A' = B, B' = (k-1)A + (k-2)B.
Solving it gives a closed form with (k-1)^(n-1) and (-1)^(n-1), divided by k.
chooseWhen: Huge n where linear DP is too slow
tradeoffs: Closed form needs a modular inverse; matrix power avoids division

constraints: up to 1000 servers with unique ids
clarifyingQuestions: What exactly are the three stress categories?
Are requests sorted by time?
What happens to requests for unknown servers?
hints: Volume and intensity are per-request constants.
Burst only depends on the same server's request times.
Sort each server's times; a request bursts if its predecessor is within 60 s or an equal time follows it.
invariants: each request contributes exactly once to exactly one server
chooseWhen: Per-key scoring with a time-window rule
tradeoffs: Sorting per server is O(n log n); bucketing by second would be O(n + 86400)
hack2hire:69753e2817272b5c868d5eb3.variantLabel: Inferred: three-part load score per server

constraints: descriptions are printable ASCII, at most 500 characters
clarifyingQuestions: Which phrases indicate each type?
What if both or neither appear?
Should the corrected array or the number of corrections be returned?
hints: Normalise case and split into words first.
'1-bedroom' becomes the words '1' and 'bedroom'.
Check single words and adjacent word pairs, then apply the exactly-one rule.
invariants: the result has the same length as the input
chooseWhen: Rule-based text normalisation
tradeoffs: Keyword rules are brittle; a classifier would need training data
